content: In the United States, activities included providing information and guidance to the industry on the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) labeling regulations. This included updates to the Nutrition Facts panel, health claims, and other FDA requirements related to food labeling. Other engagements unrelated to the topic of this guideline were not considered to pose any risk to the development of the guideline. Participation in Monsanto’s science advisory committee focused on issues related to agriculture’s role in addressing climate change and food security. Similarly, involvement with the advisory committee for the McCormick Science Institute included reviewing research proposals submitted for funding by the institute. A member of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM), she also served as a member and chair of the Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee. Her role involved reviewing evidence to develop the national dietary guidelines for the United States, known as the Dietary Guidelines for Americans. She was nominated to the Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee by representatives from various industry groups, including the North American Branch of the International Life Sciences Institute, the American Beverage Association, the American Bakers Association, the Grocery Manufacturers Association, the USA Dry Pea & Lentil Council, and the American Pulse Association. She received honorariums for presentations on the development process of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans and U.S. food labeling policies at scientific meetings organized by PMK Associates, the McCormick Institute, the Fiber Association of Japan, and the Mushroom Council. She was also a member of the Board of Trustees of the International Food Information Council (IFIC), ensuring the organization upheld its responsibilities as a 501(c)(3) non-profit entity. Additionally, she acted as a government liaison for the International Life Sciences Institute North America, where she evaluated research and organized webinars on the microbiome in 2018. In 2020, she presented a webinar to the International Dairy Foods Association on the work of the 2020 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee, specifically focusing on reducing the intake of added sodium and sugars. This webinar was unpaid. These engagements were not considered to pose any risk to the development of the guidelines. Her work on the U.S. Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee was conducted for a national authority and was therefore not considered a conflict of interest. Furthermore, her nomination to the committee by industry groups did not establish any relationship or affiliation between the nominator and the nominee. As such, these declared interests were not deemed to constitute a conflict of interest for her work with the NUGAG Subgroup on Policy Actions. Reema Tayyem declared no interests. Alison Tedstone also declared no interests. Anne Marie Thow disclosed receiving funding from the World Health Organization (WHO) for consultancies in 2015 and 2017 to analyze trade, fiscal, and nutrition policies and to support nutrition policies in Pacific Island countries. She also received funding from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and the Asian Development Bank through her university (University of Sydney) for consulting. These declarations were not considered to constitute a conflict of interest for her role in the NUGAG Subgroup on Policy Actions, given the source of the funding. Edelweiss Wentzel-Viljoen declared receiving funding from the South African Medical Research Council between 2014 and 2016 for research on salt reduction and hypertension. These declarations were not considered to pose a conflict of interest for her role in the NUGAG Subgroup on Policy Actions, given the source and topic of the funding. Elie Akl and Damian Francis declared no interests. Kathryn Angus, Angela Boland, and other members of the systematic review team also declared no interests. Emma Boyland disclosed receiving research support, including grants and sponsorships, from Cancer Research UK and the Wellcome Trust. She also provided expert opinions and testimony related to food marketing policies as part of regulatory, legislative, or judicial processes in the past three years. Additionally, she made public statements and provided positions to the UK Government Health Select Committee during the Childhood Obesity Inquiry in 2015 and 2018. These declarations were not considered to pose a conflict of interest for her role in the systematic review team, given the source of the funding. Lauren McGale declared being employed as a research assistant on the SWITCH study at the University of Liverpool, which was funded by the American Beverage Association (ABA). She clarified that the funding was awarded to the university, and she was not involved in the funding application nor named as an investigator. Her role involved recruiting participants and collecting data for the study. She did not receive any honorarium from the ABA. Her involvement in the SWITCH trial was not considered a risk to the guideline development process. External peer reviewers, including Huda Mustafa Al Hourani, Gershim Asiki, and others, declared their interests. Gershim Asiki disclosed receiving a research grant from the International Development Research Centre (IDRC) in Canada in 2019 to conduct research on the food environment and benchmarking policies in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. He also worked on mapping food promotion to children in schools, retail outlets, and on TV/radio in Kenya. These declarations were not considered to pose a conflict of interest for his role as an external peer reviewer, given the source of funding and the topics covered. Alejandro Calvillo, Suparna Ghosh-Jerath, Maria João Gregório, Fiona Sing, and Boyd Swinburn declared no interests. All declared interests were reviewed and discussed with the Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics (CRE) at WHO. Key characteristics of policies evaluated in the systematic review on the effectiveness of restricting food marketing to children were outlined. These policies varied by country and included mandatory and voluntary measures. Examples include Australia’s Children’s Television Standards, Chile’s Food Labeling and Advertising Regulation, and the UK’s content and scheduling restrictions. These policies defined marketing techniques and restrictions based on criteria such as audience composition, time of broadcast, and the use of promotional characters or incentives.
